A music student is usually taught that a piece "is in" a scale: C major, A minor, the blues scale. A scale is a list of
notes in order. Hindustani (North Indian) classical music has the word **raga**, and it is often translated "scale", but
that is not what it is. Two ragas can have exactly the same seven notes and be as different as a lullaby and a march. This
lesson shows what a raga carries that a scale does not, and lets you hear the difference.

**How to use the page.** Each widget has buttons that play. The bar at the bottom of the window sets the volume (start low).
Press *Ascent, then descent* to hear the raga; then press *As a plain scale* to hear the same notes with everything
that makes it a raga taken away.

*Unverified.* The raga descriptions below (notes, ascent and descent, vadi and samvadi, times of day) and the
Sanskrit and Hindi terms are written from general knowledge and have not been checked against a source such as Bhatkhande's
treatises or a teacher. The tuning is a modern reading of the traditional 22 notes (*shruti*) in simple ratios. Performers'
intonation depends on the raga, the singer and the tradition. Treat it as a model, and check it with a teacher who plays it.

## A scale is a list; a raga is a way of moving

Here is what a scale gives you: a set of pitches, an order, and the same order up and down. A raga gives all that, and more:

| | Scale | Raga |
|---|---|---|
| Notes | A set | A set, **but not all used equally** |
| Order | The same up and down | The **ascent (*aroha*)** and **descent (*avaroha*)** can differ: notes skipped going up, or two versions of a note |
| Which notes matter | None in particular (the tonic, perhaps) | The **vadi** (the "king": the most important note) and **samvadi** (the "minister": the second, usually a fourth or fifth from it) |
| Phrases | None | **Characteristic phrases** (*pakad*) that identify it, and rules about where to start and rest |
| Ornament | Optional | Part of the note: a slide (***meend***), a slow oscillation (***andolan***), a grace note (***kan***); together, ***gamaka*** |
| Accompaniment | Chords, perhaps | A **drone**, usually Sa and Pa, against which every note is heard |
| Time and mood | None | A time of day and a mood (*rasa*) |
| Tuning | Fixed by the instrument (the piano's) | Heard against the drone, in simple ratios; a note can have a slightly different pitch in a different raga |

The student writing a scale on paper has no place to write most of these. A raga is passed on by singing it.

## Hearing the notes of a raga

The grid at the top of each widget shows the twelve possible notes: **S r R g G M M♯ P d D n N**. Capital letters are
*shuddha* (natural), lowercase *komal* (flat), and M♯ is *tivra* Ma (sharp). A filled box is used going up and down; a box
with ▲ only going up, ▼ only coming down; a ring marks the vadi, a dashed ring the samvadi.

The first note is **Sa**, which is wherever the performer says it is, as the tonic is on any instrument. Press *Drone* to
hear Sa and Pa sustained underneath; the notes of the raga are heard against it. Choose another Sa with the second menu.

First, **Yaman**. Its notes are the major scale with a raised fourth (a Lydian scale, to a Western ear). But it begins its
ascent from the low Ni and does not rest on Sa, and the notes it dwells on are Ga and Ni:

<div class="sk" data-w="raga" data-title="Raga Yaman" data-set="raga=yaman"></div>

**Bhairav**: komal re and komal dha, with both given a slow, wide oscillation. The notes on the piano are a "double harmonic"
scale; the raga is not that scale. Press *A slide and a wobble* to hear the vadi and samvadi stepped, then joined by a slide, then
swinging:

<div class="sk" data-w="raga" data-title="Raga Bhairav" data-set="raga=bhairav"></div>

**Khamaj** is the clearest case where ascent and descent differ: leaving out Re going up, adding it coming down; and
using shuddha Ni going up but komal ni coming down:

<div class="sk" data-w="raga" data-title="Raga Khamaj" data-set="raga=khamaj"></div>

## The same notes, different ragas

Ragas with five notes show the point most cleanly. **Bhupali** and **Malkauns** each have five notes and each has the
same notes up and down. They are not the same raga as any other five-note scale you know (Bhupali is the major pentatonic, C D E G A; Malkauns, C E♭ F A♭ B♭, is a different mode of a major pentatonic, the one that starts on its third degree), and they sound different from each
other because the music dwells on different notes (the vadi) and approaches them differently:

<div class="sk" data-w="raga" data-title="Raga Bhupali" data-set="raga=bhupali"></div>

<div class="sk" data-w="raga" data-title="Raga Malkauns" data-set="raga=malkauns"></div>

And **Todi**, with its komal re, ga and dha and tivra Ma, is one of the most "bent" ragas in the repertoire:

<div class="sk" data-w="raga" data-title="Raga Todi" data-set="raga=todi"></div>

## Raga and thaat

In the twentieth century V. N. Bhatkhande sorted ragas into ten parent scales, ***thaats***, each a seven-note scale
(Bilawal, Kalyan, Khamaj, Bhairav, Poorvi, Marwa, Kafi, Asavari, Bhairavi and Todi). Yaman belongs to Kalyan, Bhairav
to Bhairav, Khamaj to Khamaj, Todi to Todi. A thaat is a scale, a filing system for ragas, and not a raga: many ragas
share one thaat, and some ragas (Bhupali and Malkauns, with five notes) fit into a thaat only by convention.
In Carnatic (South Indian) music the parent scales are the 72 ***melakartas***. *Unverified* (from memory).

## The tuning: pure ratios against a drone

The widgets tune the twelve swaras in simple ratios from Sa: re 16:15, Re 9:8, ga 6:5, Ga 5:4, Ma 4:3, M♯ 45:32,
Pa 3:2, dha 8:5, Dha 5:3, ni 16:9, Ni 15/8. On the piano the thirds, sixths and sevenths are 14 to 16 cents away
from these. Press *Raga in just tuning and on the piano, together*: the slow beating on Ga, Ni and the komal notes is that difference, and
it is a good reason that a fixed-pitch instrument is a poor way to play a raga.

The tradition has 22 pitches to the octave (*shrutis*), which does not mean twenty-two equal steps: the number
is how many distinguishable positions the notes have, and which ones a raga uses depends on it. The exact ratios, and even whether a given
shruti is 9:8 or 10:9, are argued in the literature. The page uses one common reading. See also the lessons on
[tuning systems](tuning-systems.qmd).

## Things to try

1. Play Yaman's *As a plain scale* button. What is missing from it compared to the raga?
2. In Khamaj, find the two Nis in the grid. Which is used going up, which coming down?
3. Change Sa to F♯. The notes change; what stays the same?
4. Press *Both together* in Bhairav. Which notes beat fastest? Which note does not beat at all?
5. Bhupali's vadi is Ga and Malkauns' is Ma. Hold each of those notes in turn and play the other four around it: how does the music's centre of gravity change, although both have five notes?
